### HobBogs of Dusk Reed

#### Overview

The HobBogs of Dusk Reed, known as the Deyves, are marsh folk of the most southeastern part of the Oasis Scourge. They live where red water passes under mangrove shade and where a crossing may be safe only because a household still watches it. Their marsh can feed a family for generations, but it punishes strangers who treat it like open ground.

Deyves tend to be short and wiry, with the balance of folk who spend their lives stepping from plank to root to skiff without trusting any surface for long. Their hands are narrow and strong from rope work, fish work, and the constant repair of boats. Their ears catch small changes in the marsh because a quiet insect or a wrong splash can matter more than a shouted warning.

Their skin often holds a blue-green or gray-green cast. Red mud leaves its mark on the feet and hands. Older Deyves may carry the dull stains left by years near poisoned pools. A scar is not unusual in Dusk Reed, because the marsh gives little room for careless mistakes.

Deyves wear close-fitted clothing so roots and nets do not catch them. Most clothing stays dark, with subtle variation, because color carries far through the mangrove channels. Reed fiber and treated hide are used because they endure wet labor. A wrap that has been patched many times may be valued more than new cloth, because it has already proved itself in the marsh.

A Deyve may wear a bone charm at the throat. It is not decoration. It tells the household what was survived, owed, or warned against. A shell knot can carry the memory of a crossing. A tooth can mark a debt that was paid in blood.

A Deyve does not trust the ground quickly. They test mud before giving it weight. They listen when the marsh has become too quiet. They watch still water because bad pools often look harmless at first. A pool without insects, ripples, or feeding fish may be poisoned, too deep to cross, or hiding something beneath the surface. A familiar voice from the wrong direction is treated as danger until proven otherwise.

The pole is the tool most Deyves learn first. It reads the water before the foot enters it. It steadies the body when a root shifts. It pushes a skiff through tight channels. It can also keep a snake or stranger at distance long enough for a household to decide what comes next.

A Deyve keeps a knife close because the same blade may cut rope, clean fish, or warn someone to step back. The knife is not carried as a boast. It belongs to the daily work of a place where labor can turn into violence without much warning.

Deyve homes stand above dangerous water on root-platforms and raised planks. A house must hold food beyond flood reach and keep children away from bad pools. Tools are kept where they can be found in darkness. A skiff is repaired near the same doorway where a grandmother tells children which crossings still carry old trouble.

A guest under a Deyve roof is watched closely. A guest's well-being is closely-guarded; for harm to ones gues shows weakness.

Dusk Reed began when displaced bog-folk from the east entered the enclosed swamp and made refuge there. At first, the marsh seemed hidden, defensible, and rich enough to sustain them. Then its waters began to work on them. The channels carried an unclean stain, and the folk who settled there changed slowly under its influence.

As the population grew, the Deyves looked outward. They wanted canals that would join Dusk Reed to the southern sea and to the waterways of Salt-Willow. Coral Pass and the Talirian court had been watching the migration, and they forbade the work before it could begin. No southern canal was allowed. No western canal was allowed. Dusk Reed remained enclosed.

The bog-folk became trapped with the water that had already begun to alter them. Over generations, confinement turned refuge into grievance. The marsh changed their bodies, their customs, and their sense of what the world had done to them.

That grievance shaped Deyve politics, but it did not replace ordinary life. A Deyve household still mends skiffs before dawn. Parents still teach children how to read water that looks too calm. Elders still argue over debt, memory, and medicine. The marsh made them guarded, but it did not empty them of humor or affection.

Deyves are still HobBogs; though some say that is changing. They carry the quick hands, crooked humor, and sideways speech of the bog folk. Dusk Reed has made those traits more guarded. A joke may test rank. A warning may arrive in the shape of courtesy. A child may smile at a stranger while learning whether that stranger is foolish enough to be useful.

> "Shadiness is the refuge where strength abides."

In Dusk Reed, the proverb means that concealment can keep a household alive. A Deyve who hides well may survive a stronger enemy. A Deyve who sees through hiding may gain standing. The marsh respects those who can protect food, children, and claimed ground without wasting movement.

The Deyves do not treat the marsh as a mother. They treat it as dangerous ground that can be read. It feeds those who understand its habits. It kills those who mistake beauty for safety. A Deyve learns where the marsh bites, where it feeds, and where it can be made useful.

---


#### The Land  

Dusk Reed lies in the eastern Scourge, where mangrove roots hold the land in narrow channels and broken ground. The water carries a red stain from mineral pools and old rot. Some pools only foul the skin. Others bring fever to anyone who drinks without knowing the signs.

The region is not understood by roads. A Deyve thinks in crossings. One crossing may belong to a household because that house maintains it. Another may belong to a tribe because that tribe can defend it. Some crossings are left untouched because too many folk died there for the place to be worth claiming.

Most settlements stand on root-isles. Raised planks keep sleeping places above the worst water. Mud banks become landings when the channels fall low. A bank that appears empty may still have eyes above it.

Old Siltvein families hold many of the deeper root-isles. Their authority comes from crossings that were guarded long before the Goblin Wars. The Murkwillows rose later along stronger channels. Their alliance with the Crownless King changed the balance of Dusk Reed.

The Mireborn now press the marsh toward conquest. Their blood ties them to the Crownless King and to Deyve houses that chose power over the old order. The Mangleshades survive with poorer ground and fewer claims. They endure because they know which challenge is worth making and which insult must be swallowed.

Outsiders call Dusk Reed a poisoned maze. The Deyves know it as a hard inheritance. The marsh gives fish to the patient and medicine to the careful. It gives cover to those who understand when silence matters.

#### The Goblin Wars

Dusk Reed opposed the Talirian order before the Goblin Wars reached the Scourge. The old order kept the eastern marsh contained. Coral Pass guarded the coast. Middle Vale gave force to the blockade. Salt-Willow held the western approaches and gained from the arrangement.

The Murkwillow tribe saw the Crownless King as a chance to break that order. His army could weaken Taliria in a way Dusk Reed could not achieve alone. The alliance was not built on trust. It was built on shared use.

Deyve raids struck Salt-Willow during the war. Those raids drew attention away from other movements. They also proved that Dusk Reed could carry violence through channels that outsiders struggled to read. The Crownless King gained time because the marsh knew how to hide a war.

After the Goblin army broke, the Crownless King remained in Dusk Reed. He could not return safely to his old lands. In the marsh he became a fugitive ruler with dangerous value. He took Deyve wives, and his descendants became the Mireborn.

The Mireborn changed Dusk Reed. Their rise weakened older balances between tribes. The Murkwillows gained power from the new bloodline. The Siltveins lost part of their old authority. The Mangleshades were pushed farther into the margins.

Dusk Reed also learned to use the Pale Hymn. The doctrine gave captives a new order and gave Dusk Reed a way to reshape them. The Verdant Glenkin taken through war were remade as the Ashverin. Their new identity served Dusk Reed’s western design.

Glentali Lake became the proof of that design. War had damaged its fields and crossings. The returning Dellari were scattered and weak. The Ashverin entered with doctrine behind them and began to take root where Dellari memory had been broken.

Within a generation, Glentali produced food again. It did so under a new people and a new story. Dusk Reed had escaped confinement and learned how to rule through others.

---

#### Tradition and Lore

Deyve lore teaches survival before comfort. Stories are told beside low fires and marked door-posts. A good story tells a child when to doubt a voice. It teaches them to read the mud before answering love.

The Backward Walker is one of the oldest terrors in Dusk Reed. It moves beyond the roots with its feet turned the wrong way. It calls in a voice that should be trusted. A child may hear a dead sister. A hunter may hear a lost mate. The voice is bait, and the mud gives the warning.

<div class="lore-scroll" markdown="1">

In the old telling, a young Deyve heard his dead sister calling from beyond the roots.

She had drowned three seasons before, but her voice came soft through the mangroves.

"Bring the pole," she said. "The mud has my ankle."

His mother stood by the house-fire and told him not to answer.

The voice called again.

This time it used his childhood name.

The boy stepped to the first root and stopped. In the mud beyond it, he saw small footprints. They looked like hers. They were wrong. The toes faced him, but the heel marks led away.

His mother did not warn him again. She placed a knife in his hand and watched.

The boy followed beside the tracks instead of inside them. He read drag, weight, broken reed, and water pull. The voice grew sweeter. Then it grew angry. Then it grew hungry.

At the red pool, something rose from the mangrove shade wearing his sister's sound. Its feet bent backward under wet hair. Its mouth opened with her voice.

The boy threw the knife into the voice instead of the body.

The thing broke like rotten bark. The pool swallowed it.

When he returned, his mother pressed red mud beneath the threshold.

"Now the house knows you," she said.

From that day, the children learned to read mud before love.

</div>

The Bride Beneath the Roots belongs to another old tale. She appears near still pools before raids, fevers, or betrayals. Some households believe she warns the strong. Others believe she calls the weak into water. No version makes her safe.

These stories shape daily practice. A child learns to study footprints before trusting a cry for help. A skiff may carry a root charm against false voices. A household that survives betrayal may carve backward feet beneath the door-post. The mark tells visitors that deception came there and was answered.

---

#### Swamping

Swamping is the work of taking a living from Dusk Reed. The work feeds the house and repairs the skiff. It also teaches danger, because the marsh rarely separates food from risk.

A skilled swamper knows which pools can be touched. They know which vapors can sicken the lungs. They know when a root will hold weight. They know when mud has loosened beneath a thin skin of water.

The marsh gives fish to those who know the channels. It gives eel to those who know when the water turns. Alligator meat feeds a house when the hunt goes well. Red reeds become fiber after careful cutting. Bitter fungus becomes medicine only when prepared correctly.

Venom has value in Dusk Reed, but it is not handled casually. A careless poisoner can ruin a cure or kill someone useful. A careful one may keep a household alive through sickness or make an enemy afraid to touch a cup.

Goods pass first through the household. The family eats before trade begins. The skiff is repaired before tribute is sent. A hidden store may matter more than a public gift when bad water ruins a season.

Swamping trains the eye as much as the hand. A broken reed can show recent passage. A still pool can warn of sickness. A sour smell can mark bad water ahead. A root-scratch can guide a friend or mislead a pursuer.

Ordinary work fills the hours between dangers. Cooking smoke rises from sheltered fire-pits. Hide scrapers begin before the heat climbs. Skiff boards are sealed before raiding season. Children learn which clay pots near the elder’s post must not be opened.

A good swamper earns respect because attention keeps the household alive. They can feed a house through bad water. They can tell when medicine has become poison. In Dusk Reed, useful knowledge is a form of strength.

---

#### Morality and Social Bonds

Deyve morality begins with the household. A deed is judged by what it protects. It is also judged by what obligation follows. The same act can mean one thing for kin and another thing for a stranger.

Family must be protected. A child belongs within the strength of the house. A mate must be defended before outsiders. An elder remains valuable because memory can save lives. A household that leaves its own exposed loses standing.

Deyves do not treat kindness as simple. A favor can create claim. A rescue can create debt. Food given during hunger may return later as labor or silence. A gift can bind a person because everyone remembers who needed it.

Tribal bonds are harder than household bonds. A Deyve may quarrel inside the tribe. They may scheme for rank. Ambition is expected, but betrayal before outsiders stains a name. Cruelty may be forgiven if it protects the tribe. Exposure is harder to forgive.

Strangers stand outside most obligations until a household claims them. A merchant may be tolerated because trade is useful. A trespasser may be punished because punishment teaches others. Mercy can be shown, but it usually has a purpose.

Guest-right exists in Dusk Reed. A guest under a roof is watched, fed, and protected while the roof holds over them. This protection is not softness. It shows that the household can answer for its own space.

---

#### Speech and Dialect

Deyve speech keeps the old HobBog rhythm, but the rhythm has hardened. Words bend around rank and debt. A listener must hear what is being claimed as much as what is being said.

The running "s" appears often in ordinary speech. A Deyve may say, "Muds waitings for a foot." The phrase can warn a child or insult a stranger. When anger rises, the final sound may land harder. "Muds waitings for a foots" is closer to threat.

Deyve sayings are practical. A hidden rival may be called "roots with teeths." A patient enemy may be described as "still waters holdings hunger under." A fool who talks too much may be "a frog singings for the herons." A frightened liar has "fears showings through the reeds."

Conversation tests position. A simple question can ask who owns a crossing. It can ask who owes a debt. It can ask who has the right to speak first. Repetition gives the speaker time to measure the answer.

Affection is guarded but present. A mother may say, "You's stood good." She means pride and expectation at once. A mate may say, "I keeps your knifes dry." The words are plain, but the promise is intimate.

To speak like a Deyve is to speak with consequence. The words carry feeling, but they also carry claim.

---

#### Marriage and Family

Deyve courtship begins with proof. Beauty may draw attention, but pressure reveals value. A steady hand in bad water matters. A clean answer to insult matters. A dangerous crossing held without panic may speak more clearly than open affection.

Love among the Deyves is tied to standing. A partner is judged by what they strengthen in the household. They are also judged by what danger they keep away from it. Desire alone is not trusted for long.

Family bonds carry duty. A mate is defended and tested. A household may use a marriage to settle old debt. A strong joining can secure a passage. A weak joining can lower the standing of both houses.

Marriage gifts show control as much as generosity. A family may offer a weapon because it has strength to spare. A poison store may show access to guarded knowledge. A skiff share may show control over movement. A hidden landing may be the most valuable gift of all.

The joining is witnessed by elders and speakers whose debts are touched by the bond. The couple may stand beside a marked channel. They may stand at a root-post or near a low fire. Names are spoken so no witness can pretend confusion later.

A common marriage sign is the held passage. The pair crosses a narrow plank or root-bridge together. The crossing means they agree to hold one path through hunger and insult. If either stumbles, the witnesses remember. If both cross cleanly, the bond begins with approval.

Deyve marriages can hold affection. That affection usually stays guarded in public. A good union does not make either partner softer. It gives the household more force.

Among the Deyves, marriage is not escape from struggle. It is a pact to survive with stronger hands.

---

#### Children and Games  

Deyve children grow under watch. Older eyes measure how much danger a child can be trusted to carry. A young’un learns which pools sicken. They learn which roots hold weight. They learn which voices should not be answered from the dark.

Play teaches position. A chase through the mangroves can become a test of hiding. A balance game on wet roots can become a test of nerve. A hiding game can become serious when one child claims a crossing.

One common game is called **Backward Walker**. Children mark false tracks in mud. They turn the signs the wrong way to confuse the seeker. The seeker must read drag and weight rather than shape. A child who reads the mud correctly earns praise.

Other games teach claim. Young’uns build small crossings from sticks. They argue over who owns the passage. They stain skiff scraps red and dare one another to touch sickly water with a pole-tip. They answer from behind roots so others learn not to trust an easy voice.

Deyve childhood is full of training disguised as play. The games teach fear, command, debt, and attention. A child who learns slowly may still be loved, but the marsh will not slow itself for them.

In Dusk Reed, a game is rarely only a game for long.

---

#### Death and Memory

Deyves believe the dead sink into the red mud beneath Dusk Reed.

At death, the final breath is taken by the marsh. The body returns through root and silt. The dead do not drift away from the household. They remain in the places their lives helped hold.

A strong death leaves weight behind. A feared mother may remain in the pool where she was returned. A raider may cling to the crossing named for him. A sick child who endured may be remembered at the door-post.

Deyves speak carefully near burial mud. They do not turn the dead into comfort. A good dead one should still have force. The dead may guard a claim or sour an enemy’s path. They may strengthen a household by reminding the living what must not be wasted.

After death, families may press red mud onto a skiff rail. They may mark a door-post with it. The mark does not ask the dead to rest. It asks them to remain useful.

To the Deyves, death is possession carried deeper. The body returns to the marsh. The name remains with the household. The strongest dead abide where their folk still dare to stand.

---

#### Songs

Dusk Reed songs make fear useful. A song can steady the hand before a raid. It can keep a child alert near bad water. It can carry warning without raising the voice.

Many Deyve songs are low because sound travels strangely through the roots. A raiding song may begin beneath the oars. It may tighten as the skiffs near a landing. A household song may praise someone by naming what they held when others failed.

Children’s songs carry the Backward Walker through the roots. The verses teach wrong tracks and false voices. A playful tune can turn cruel by the final line. The child learns that laughter ends quickly when the marsh answers back.

Work songs belong to poison-making and skiff repair. Their rhythms keep the hands steady. A root-fiber chant may teach a child when to tighten a knot. A poison song may count drops without saying too much aloud.

War songs rose after the Goblin Wars. Murkwillow singers praise hidden channels and decoy raids. Songs about the Crownless King claim that he broke the old order open. Mireborn songs are harsher because conquest is part of their inheritance.

Deyve songs rarely seek comfort. They honor the feared and mock the careless. A song can make a crossing into a warning. It can make a pool into a judge. It can make a voice in the mangroves into the last thing a fool follows.

#### Recap Table


```{r}

recap_table <- data.frame(
  Section = c(
    "Overview",
    "The Land",
    "The Goblin Wars",
    "Tradition and Lore",
    "Swamping",
    "Morality and Social Bonds",
    "Speech and Dialect",
    "Marriage and Family",
    "Children and Games",
    "Death and Memory",
    "Songs"
  ),
  `Dusk Reed Deyves` = c(
    "Eastern HobBog folk who survive through guarded crossings, household strength, and careful reading of poisoned water.",
    "A mangrove marsh where root-isles hold settlements and safe crossings belong to those who can defend them.",
    "Dusk Reed aided the Crownless King, rose through the Murkwillows, and later used the Ashverin to reshape Glentali Lake.",
    "Deyve lore teaches children to distrust false voices and read the mud before answering love.",
    "Swamping turns marsh knowledge into food, medicine, poison, passage, and household strength.",
    "Deyve morality begins with the household and treats every favor as a possible obligation.",
    "Deyve speech keeps HobBog rhythm while carrying rank, debt, threat, and claim.",
    "Marriage is a public bond of proof, household standing, guarded affection, and shared survival.",
    "Young’uns learn through games that teach tracking, claim, fear, and attention.",
    "The dead sink into red mud and remain useful through household memory.",
    "Songs steady work, teach fear, preserve war memory, and sharpen warnings."
  ),
  check.names = FALSE
)

kbl(
  recap_table,
  caption = "Recap Table",
  align = c("l", "l"),
  escape = FALSE
) %>%
  kable_styling(
    full_width = TRUE,
    bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed")
  ) %>%
  column_spec(1, width = "12em", bold = TRUE) %>%
  column_spec(2, width = "60em")



```
